The biggest for me was one of my first. The year was 2001, the game: Pools of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor, a Dungeons and Dragons RPG for PC.

You see, PC DnD games had just experienced a renaissance, much like today: several huge titles like Baldurs Gate 1 and 2 and Icewind Dale 1 and 2, not to mention Planescape: Torment, had raised the bar for CRPGs in general. The issue with these games, though, was that they did not reflect the current state of DnD, which had, in 2000, jumped from the classic 2nd Edition to the new and shiny 3rd Edition. The difference between these versions of the game, if you are unfamiliar, is kind of like... the difference between the old Star Trek movies and the new ones. It's pretty huge.

So anyway, I went in for the super deluxe collector's edition of the game, which included all types of nerd shit like a felt dice bag, a printed adventure, a gigantic box, maybe some other crap. I didn't even have a computer capable of playing the game but I wanted to play it so bad I bought it anyway to play on a friend's PC.

The game came out and it was utter broken shit. The wikipedia entry sums it up pretty well:

It received lackluster reviews and was plagued with bugs. One major bug would cause a player's system files to uninstall when the game was removed.[7] Other bugs included problems with installation, saving game files, graphics, and gameplay.[2] Chris Chan of the New Straits Times complained that most of the game is spent "[engaged] with a lot of mindless battles and health and spell recuperation exercises."[1] Mark Meadows of The Wisconsin State Journal called the game: "A half-finished adaptation of D&D's new 3rd Edition rules that was rushed out the door despite being over a year late."[2] GameSpy's review suggested: "If you see this game, walk away … really fast!"[8] Later patches fixed some of the stability issues.[1] Branislav Babovic of mania.com commented: "Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor could simply be defined as a disk full of bugs, striving to be a slow Diablo based on AD&D third edition rules."

This was just after Electronics Boutique (pre-Gamestop) had initiated it's No Return policy on PC games, so they wouldn't take it back. I contacted the publisher and they told me to deal with the retailer and were unsympathetic when I explained the retailer was unwilling to refund me. It was the first time I felt totally fucked by the industry that I loved and supported and I felt totally helpless. It also marks the first time, waaaay back in 2001, that I went online to a game forum and joined in the angry mob. I got some forum notoriety for claiming that I would become a game developer myself just so that someday I could meet the developer at a conference and hand the game back to them with a dead squirrel and a human bowel movement inside so that they could have the same experience upon opening it that I did.

The developer was Stormfront Studios, which was actually a pretty good studio; my issue was clearly with publisher Ubisoft for forcing the game's release in an unfinished (and potentially hazardous) state. But 14 years ago I was not the jaded monster the last decade and a half of disappointments has made me, now I know better...

I still would've shit in the box and handed it to them but I would've kept the dead squirrel out of it.

WoD did better than Cata, but not by much. It also removed so much about the game that made it worth playing (in my opinion). Removing a third of the spells and abilities made all the classes seem less different and unique. Removing the gear jump between expansions was the worst change in my opinion. I'm an altoholic. I level alts more than I do anything else. And changing it so that you don't experience those jumps in power killed that joy for me. I always looked forward to reaching level 58, 68, 78, etc. because new gear was available that was 100 ilvl above what I was wearing and it would greatly increase my damage potential. It was fun to have that little boost of power.

Aside from those changes, the expansion added the worst feature to the game: Garrisons. Garrisons are essentially prison cells for your character. You're cut off from the rest of the game except for trade chat (which isn't exactly a perk). Your character is forced to do chores like mining, herb gathering, mission management, and collecting boxes of trade goods. Your followers are out doing the adventures and raids that you should be doing. It was an interesting idea but very poorly implemented. Most people log in these days to do garrison chores, sit around for a bit chatting, and then log out. And unlike cities, you can't see other players in their garrisons (unless invited). So the world became very empty. People wanted player housing for so long without realizing it was a terrible idea. It's only useful to introverts.

The other problem with WoD is that they're cutting it in half. It's ending only halfway into the expansion. They confirmed patch 6.2 was the final patch of the expansion. All other expansions reached at least x.4.x before ending. This is due to players being burnt out with the lack of content. So they're very likely going to rush a new expansion which will still lack content like WoD did, which will cause them to end it prematurely and force another unfinished expansion down the line, ad nausea.

World of Warcraft has been hemorrhaging subscribers for months. It surged up 3 million after WoD released but only a month or two later that 3 million had left again, due to the lack of content.

If they aim to save the game, they need to develop a well thought out expansion that will reignite players' love for the game. Another Wrath of the Lich King or Burning Crusade. Not this shoveled shit. WLK was the high point in the game, followed by the low point in the game. I wish they had realized their mistakes in Cata and not repeat them in MoP and WoD. We were stuck in Siege of Orgrimmar for over a year. Now they're trying to make up for that burn out by forcing unfinished content at us rapidly. Wildstar.

I was coming from a series of disappointments because of 3 games I loved going free to play over time and losing the quality focus in favor of the cash shop, last one being Rift (the most shady transition I've experienced), and also some changes I didn't like in other games.

So I welcomed Wildstar, it looked very promising, challenging enough, fun, communication from the devs was also very good, so I preordered it and started to play during the beta weekends (about 1 month).
What I liked is that they promised content for different kind of playstyle, hardcore raids but also story for non raiders.

During the beta people pointed out what was considered a big flaw in game design, a source of potential problems, that was how the AMP system was designed.
AMPs are the equivalent of talent points, a core mechanic in all MMORPGs that's vital to your character development.

Most people on the beta forum agreed that abilities and talent points should be automatically earned while you level up, ALL of them, and by the time you reach level cap you should have everything you need to setup your build and play, and then leave the grind to things like gear, upgrades, crafting professions and fluff (housing would have been the perfect time and gold sink).

But it wasn't like that in Wildstar.
You could get all your basic abilities and most talent points by leveling, then you had to acquire the rest by other means, some were gated behind faction reps, some were random world drops, you had to grind for gold to be able to buy some from AH, and so on.
That would have created an unfair disparity between people and a nightmare to play alts, not considering how punishing it would have been for new players joining after months or years, with no way to catch up in a reasonable amount of time.

There was a sort of megathread on the forum with a lot of good feedback that has been ignored.

Then the game came out and those reaching level cap first started to report a hell lot of bugs that made playing end content almost impossible, they were slow to fix them and also the promised content for non raiders didn't exist.

On top of that it turned out the devs had a very arrogant attitude and instead of listening to suggestions they were over reacting on very stupid things. 2 examples:

  • People complained that the inventory bag given with the deluxe edition was too small. Instead of ignoring such a stupid complaint, or maybe make the bag a bit bigger, they put level restrictions on ALL bags in the game and also restrictions on crafted ones so you could only equip one!
    Not only that made players life miserable because you could only have decent bags at high levels (and inventory is always a problem in every MMO), but also defeated the purpose of working hard to level crafting (everyone needs bags so that's always a healthy market in every game).

  • Another example was the outfit system. If was very good at first, you had a lot of freedom. It worked exacly like Rift, you equipped pieces into outfit slots (unlike LoTRO and SWTOR in which you just copy the appearance). You could change your appearance anywhere.
    Then is seems people were using it to put real gear into it to save a few bag slots because of the miserable restrictions so they took the freedom away.

There were also several other little annoyances, that added together and on top of what I described already, disheartened people so they started to leave in drones.
I lost faith in the game and left as well.

A year has passed and people who gave the game another try are now saying good things about it. It seems the direction has changed and the promised non raider content has come.

It'll go free to play in Autumn, I guess it won't be different from the 3 transitions I've experienced already, so I'm a bit on the fence about it.

There are no plans to remove/widen the container. The only solution is to zoom in.

Depends really.

What platform would you be playing on?

What kind of game is it?

did the game get shipped with a graphics card?

How popular is the game, how often is it selling?

All important factors. Games for a younger audience are usually cheaper on PC (Lego titles for example), PC also tends to have more stingy customers who won't buy at a lower price, ergo, more sales. If it's shipped with graphics cards, the price will drop dramatically very quick.

Depends on how well the game initially sold, and who published it, EA will milk the game for all it's worth (Dragon Age dropped to $10, but the individual DLC is still being sold at full price, for those people who just got the regular game), I normally wait for Steam holiday specials, or digital sales. Other than that game of the year editions/ultimate editions are anywhere from six months to a year after release, which at full price saves you throwing $30-$50 at DLC alone (except Mass Effect 3, even in the trilogy pack it's missing a chunk of content), and then a few months after that the game loses $10 every quarter of the year or so down to a minimum of $10 if the game hits the three-five year mark.
